title: The minimum variance portfolio
objectives: Find the minimum variance two-asset portfolio with a Lagrange multiplier.
Check the answer by substitution and see how correlation moves it.

screens.title: The least risky mix
screens.prose: Asset A has volatility 20% and asset B 10%. Their returns have correlation 0.3. You put a fraction $w_1$ of your money in A and the rest in B. The curve is the portfolio volatility $\sigma_p$.

derive.caption: In A: {{fixed(w * 100, 1)}}%. Portfolio volatility: {{fixed(sqrt(max(0, w*w*s1*s1 + (1 - w)*(1 - w)*s2*s2 + 2*w*(1 - w)*r*s1*s2)) * 100, 2)}}%

screens.question: Set $w_1$ to the mix with the lowest volatility.

hints.text: Watch the volatility in the caption as you slide towards 0.
Near $w_1 = 0$ the curve dips just below the B-alone line.
The lowest volatility, 9.79%, comes at about 10.5% in A.

feedback.correct: About 10.5% in A, for a volatility of 9.79%.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide towards 0 and watch for the lowest volatility in the caption.

byKey.all-b: You put everything, or nearly everything, in B. A little of A lowers the risk: at 10.5% in A it is 9.79%.
byKey.half: Half and half gives 12.45%. The risk keeps falling as you move towards B, until about 10.5% in A.
byKey.all-a: A alone has 20% volatility, the riskiest choice here.

explain.text: You found the lowest point at about 10.5% in A, with volatility 9.79%. That is below B alone, though A is twice as volatile. Because the two do not move in lockstep, a little A partly cancels B's swings.

screens.title: Changing the correlation
screens.prose: Same two assets, but now you set the correlation $\rho$. The marked point is the lowest point of the curve with $w_1$ between 0 and 1.
screens.question: Set $\rho = -1$. What is the lowest volatility you can reach?

widget.label: Lowest volatility
widget.accept: 0%, with a third of the money in A.

hints.text: Drag the $\rho$ slider all the way to the left.
Watch where the marked point lands.

feedback.correct: Zero: the two assets cancel exactly.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set $\rho = -1$ and read the caption.

byKey.b: That is B alone. With $\rho = -1$ the curve drops all the way to the axis.
byKey.base: That is the lowest point at $\rho = 0.3$. Move the slider to $-1$ first.

explain.text: At $\rho = -1$ the assets move exactly opposite. With a third in A, $\tfrac{1}{3} \times 20\% = \tfrac{2}{3} \times 10\%$, so their swings cancel and the risk is zero. As $\rho$ rises, the dip shrinks; from $\rho = 0.5$ up, B alone is best.

screens.title: The minimum variance portfolio
screens.prose: The least risky mix is the **minimum variance portfolio**. The variance is $$\sigma_p^2 = w_1^2\sigma_1^2 + w_2^2\sigma_2^2 + 2w_1w_2\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2.$$ With $w_2 = 1 - w_1$, $\sigma_1 = 0.2$, $\sigma_2 = 0.1$, $\rho = 0.3$, it becomes $a w_1^2 + b w_1 + 0.01$.
screens.question: What is the coefficient $a$?

hints.text: Collect the $w_1^2$ terms from all three parts.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each of the three terms contributes to $w_1^2$.

byKey.nocross: You took $0.04 + 0.01$ but left out the cross term. $2w_1(1 - w_1)(0.006)$ contributes $-0.012w_1^2$.
byKey.first: $(1 - w_1)^2\sigma_2^2$ also contributes $0.01w_1^2$, and the cross term $-0.012w_1^2$.

explain.text: Expanding gives $0.04w_1^2 + 0.01(1 - 2w_1 + w_1^2) + 0.012(w_1 - w_1^2)$. Collecting terms: $\sigma_p^2 = 0.038w_1^2 - 0.008w_1 + 0.01$. A parabola opening upwards, as drawn.

screens.title: Setting the slope to zero
screens.prose: So $\sigma_p^2 = 0.038w_1^2 - 0.008w_1 + 0.01$. Its lowest point is where the derivative is zero.
screens.question: Solve $\dfrac{d\sigma_p^2}{dw_1} = 0$. What is $w_1$? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: Differentiate: $\tfrac{d}{dw_1}(aw_1^2 + bw_1 + c) = 2aw_1 + b$.
Drag the point until the tangent is flat.

byKey.notwo: You solved $0.038w_1 = 0.008$. The derivative of $0.038w_1^2$ is $0.076w_1$.
byKey.zero: At $w_1 = 0$ the slope is $-0.008$, so the variance still falls as you add A.
byKey.ratio: That is $\sigma_2^2 / \sigma_1^2$, which ignores the correlation. Solve the derivative instead.

explain.text: The derivative $0.076w_1 - 0.008$ is zero at $w_1 = 0.10526$. There $\sigma_p^2 = 0.0095789$, so $\sigma_p = 0.09787$: 9.79%. The tangent is flat at the bottom of the parabola.

screens.title: The same answer with a multiplier
screens.prose: Treat $w_1$ and $w_2$ as free, with the budget $w_1 + w_2 = 1$ as a constraint. The ellipses are contours of $\sigma_p^2$. Here $$\nabla \sigma_p^2 = (0.08w_1 + 0.012w_2,\ 0.02w_2 + 0.012w_1).$$
screens.question: Solve $\nabla \sigma_p^2 = \lambda (1, 1)$ with $w_1 + w_2 = 1$. What is $w_2$? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: Both components equal $\lambda$, so set them equal to each other.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Equate the two components, then use $w_1 + w_2 = 1$.

byKey.w1: That is $w_1$, the weight in A. The question asks for $w_2$, the weight in B.
byKey.half: Equal weights ignore the gradient equations. They give $w_2 = 8.5w_1$.
byKey.ratio: 8.5 is the ratio $w_2 / w_1$. Use the budget $w_1 + w_2 = 1$ to turn it into weights.

explain.text: Equating the components gave $w_2 = 8.5w_1$, and the budget gave $w_1 = 0.1053$, $w_2 = 0.8947$: the same as substitution. The purple ellipse touches the budget line there. The multiplier is $\lambda = 0.01916$, exactly $2\sigma_p^2$.

screens.title: Perfect correlation
screens.prose: Now let $\rho = 1$, with no short sales, so $0 \le w_1 \le 1$. Then $\sigma_p = w_1\sigma_1 + w_2\sigma_2$ exactly: a straight line from 10% to 20%.
screens.question: Which mix has the lowest volatility?

options.why: The formula gives $(0.01 - 0.02)/(0.04 + 0.01 - 0.04) = -1$: a short sale of A. With $0 \le w_1 \le 1$, the line's lowest point is its end.
On a straight line there is no dip in the middle. Half in each gives 15%.
The volatility still changes with the mix: it climbs from 10% to 20% along the line.

hints.text: Where is a rising straight line lowest?
The line starts at B alone.
With $\rho = 1$ there is no dip: the lowest volatility, 10%, is at $w_1 = 0$.

feedback.correct: All in B: with $\rho = 1$ mixing gives no benefit.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. With $\rho = 1$ the volatility is a straight line in $w_1$.

explain.text: With $\rho = 1$ the assets move in lockstep, so mixing only averages their volatilities. The best long-only mix is a corner, all in B. With short sales, $w_1 = -1$ would hedge the risk away entirely.

screens.title: The calmer asset alone
screens.prose: Asset A has volatility 30% and asset B 15%, uncorrelated. A colleague says the safest portfolio is all in B, the calmer asset.

state.caption: The volatility curve appears after you answer.

screens.question: What is the lowest volatility you can reach?

options.why: You held only the calmer asset. With $\rho = 0$, adding some A lowers the risk: 20% in A gives 13.4%.
Zero risk needs $\rho = -1$. Uncorrelated assets cannot cancel exactly.
You averaged the volatilities. Half and half gives $\sqrt{0.25 \times 0.09 + 0.25 \times 0.0225} = 16.8\%$, and less A does better.

hints.text: Use $w_1^* = \dfrac{\sigma_2^2 - \rho\sigma_1\sigma_2}{\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 - 2\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2}$ with $\rho = 0$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find $w_1^*$ with $\rho = 0$, then the volatility there.

byKey.allb: You assumed the least risky asset is the least risky portfolio. Unless $\rho$ is high, a slice of the riskier asset diversifies.

explain.text: With $\rho = 0$, $w_1^* = 0.0225 / 0.1125 = 0.2$ and $\sigma_p^2 = 0.0036 + 0.0144 = 0.018$, so $\sigma_p = 13.4\%$. The curve dips below B alone. The calmer asset on its own is not the least risky portfolio.

screens.title: The formula
screens.prose: Solving either way, for any $\sigma_1$, $\sigma_2$ and $\rho$: $$w_1^* = \frac{\sigma_2^2 - \rho\sigma_1\sigma_2}{\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 - 2\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2}, \qquad w_2^* = 1 - w_1^*.$$ With no short sales, clip $w_1^*$ to the range 0 to 1.
screens.question: Check it on the first pair: $\sigma_1 = 0.2$, $\sigma_2 = 0.1$, $\rho = 0.3$. What is the numerator?

hints.text: $\sigma_2^2 = 0.01$ and $\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2 = 0.3 \times 0.2 \times 0.1$.

byKey.s1: You used $\sigma_1^2 = 0.04$. The numerator for $w_1$ uses the other asset's variance, $\sigma_2^2$.

explain.text: The numerator is $0.01 - 0.006 = 0.004$ and the denominator $0.038$, so $w_1^* = 0.1053$. Notice the numerator uses the *other* asset's variance: the calmer asset gets the larger weight.

screens.title: Deriving the formula
screens.prose: We minimise $\sigma_p^2$ over $w_1$, with $w_2 = 1 - w_1$. Write $\sigma_1, \sigma_2, \rho$ as letters throughout.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $\dfrac{d\sigma_p^2}{dw_1} = 2w_1\sigma_1^2 - 2(1 - w_1)\sigma_2^2 + 2(1 - 2w_1)\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2$, chain rule and product rule
$0 = w_1\sigma_1^2 - \sigma_2^2 + w_1\sigma_2^2 + \rho\sigma_1\sigma_2 - 2w_1\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2$, set it to zero, halve and expand

hints.text: Substitute first, then differentiate.
Collecting the $w_1$ terms needs the expanded equation.
Substitute, differentiate, set to zero and expand, collect, divide.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. You must substitute $w_2 = 1 - w_1$ before differentiating in $w_1$.

byKey.collect: Collecting needs the expanded form, so the zero line comes first.
byKey.divide: Dividing is the last step, once all $w_1$ terms are on one side.

explain.text: One derivative, set to zero, gives a linear equation in $w_1$. The bracket we divide by is $\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 - 2\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2$, the variance of $R_A - R_B$. It is positive unless the assets are identical, so the formula always works.

screens.title: A long-only mandate
screens.prose: A fund holds two equity books: A with volatility 15%, B with 25%, correlation 0.8. The formula gives $w_1^* = 1.3$: 130% in A and −30% in B. The fund's mandate bans short sales.

state.caption: Dashed lines: the allowed weights, 0 to 1

screens.question: Which weight $w_1$ should the fund hold?

widget.label: w1
widget.accept: 1: all in A, the allowed weight nearest 1.3.

hints.text: The allowed weights lie between the two dashed lines.
Between 0 and 1, the curve falls all the way to the right-hand line.
The variance is a parabola with its lowest point at 1.3. On $[0, 1]$ it is lowest at the end nearest 1.3: $w_1 = 1$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the lowest point of the curve between 0 and 1.

byKey.ignore: 1.3 breaks the mandate: it needs a short position of 30% in B.
byKey.zero: All in B is the riskiest allowed choice here, at 25%.
byKey.half: Half in each gives about 19%. The curve keeps falling towards $w_1 = 1$.

explain.text: The variance is a parabola in $w_1$ with its lowest point at 1.3. Restricted to $[0, 1]$, it is lowest at $w_1 = 1$: all in A, volatility 15%. Clipping the formula to the allowed range always gives the long-only answer for two assets.

ideas: With $w_2 = 1 - w_1$ the portfolio variance is a parabola in $w_1$. Its lowest point is the minimum variance portfolio.
A multiplier on $w_1 + w_2 = 1$ gives the same weights, with $\lambda = 2\sigma_p^2$ at the minimum.
Lower correlation means a deeper dip: at $\rho = -1$ risk can reach zero, at $\rho = 1$ there is no dip. A ban on short sales clips $w_1$ to $[0, 1]$.
summary.trap: The least volatile asset alone is not the least volatile portfolio. Unless correlation is high, a slice of the riskier asset lowers risk.

quiz.prose: Two assets both have volatility 20%, with correlation 0.5.
quiz.question: What weight $w_1$ gives the minimum variance portfolio?

widget.label: w1
widget.accept: 0.5, by symmetry or from the formula.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. With equal volatilities the formula's top is half its bottom.

byKey.zero: Neither asset is calmer, so neither corner wins. Splitting evenly diversifies.
byKey.one: Neither asset is calmer, so neither corner wins. Splitting evenly diversifies.

explain.text: $w_1^* = (0.04 - 0.02)/(0.04 + 0.04 - 0.04) = 0.02/0.04 = 0.5$. Identical volatilities make the assets interchangeable, so the best split is even.

quiz.prose: Asset A has volatility 20% and B 10%, with correlation $-1$.
quiz.question: Which weight in A makes the portfolio riskless?

options.why: Half and half leaves A's larger swings uncancelled: $0.5 \times 20\% - 0.5 \times 10\% = 5\%$.
You gave the larger weight to the riskier asset. A needs the smaller weight.
With $\rho = -1$ the swings can cancel exactly.

explain.text: With $\rho = -1$, $\sigma_p = |0.2w_1 - 0.1(1 - w_1)|$, which is zero when $0.3w_1 = 0.1$. So $w_1 = \tfrac{1}{3}$, matching the formula: $0.03 / 0.09$.

quiz.question: What is $\sigma_p^2$ for half in each asset?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each weight is 0.5, so each squared weight is 0.25.

byKey.avg: You averaged the variances. The weights enter squared: $0.25 \times 0.04 + 0.25 \times 0.01 + 0.003$.

quiz.prose: Two assets, no short sales. B is the less volatile of the two.
quiz.question: Which statement is always true?

options.text: The minimum variance portfolio is never riskier than B alone
The minimum variance portfolio is all in B
options.why: Only when $\rho \ge \sigma_B / \sigma_A$. Otherwise some A lowers the risk further.

options.text: The minimum variance portfolio has zero risk
The minimum variance portfolio holds more of A than of B
options.why: The calmer asset gets the larger weight: the numerator of $w_A$ uses $\sigma_B^2$.

feedback.correct: All in B is one of the choices, so the best can only match or beat it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which choices the minimum is taken over.

explain.text: All in B is an allowed portfolio, so the lowest variance over all allowed mixes is at most B's variance. It equals it when $\rho \ge \sigma_B / \sigma_A$, and beats it otherwise.
